actual_action: Morton Thiokol management reversed the initial engineering recommendation and recommended launch; STS-51L launched the next morning.
later_evidence: The Rogers Commission later found that the launch decision process was flawed and that key senior decision-makers were unaware of the initial contractor no-launch recommendation and continuing engineering opposition.
NASA's historical mission record identifies failure of a right solid-rocket-booster O-ring, aggravated by extreme cold, as the accident cause.

McDonald's typed account, numbered note page 9 (Rogers Commission Volume IV, printed p. 744), records his explicit discomfort while awaiting the signed fax, after Thiokol had orally recommended launch. That reaction is excluded from the candidate's pre-recommendation packet; the earlier sealing objection and local delay proposal remain separately attributed.
outcomes: Challenger was lost 73 seconds after liftoff.
The accident triggered extensive investigation and changes to shuttle safety and decision processes.
later_reviews_or_findings: The Rogers Commission concluded that Thiokol management reversed its position, contrary to engineers' views, to accommodate a major customer.
The Commission found communication failures and a management structure that allowed serious safety concerns to bypass key launch managers.
The Commission criticised launch-constraint waivers and the treatment of incomplete/inconclusive safety information.
